title: Interface Module
body:
The file pair that packages a [[Class]] so other programs can use it. The course's three-file
layout:

| File | Holds | Who reads it |
|---|---|---|
| `intstack.h` | the class declaration: the [[Interface]] | the client, and you |
| `intstack.cpp` | the member function bodies: the [[Implementation]] | only you |
| `main.cpp` | the [[Client Program]] | the person solving the actual problem |

The header and the `.cpp` together are the **interface module**. The client `#include`s the
header and never touches the second file.

```c++
// main.cpp
#include "intstack.h"     // quotes for your own files, <> for the standard library
int main() {
	IntStack s;
	s.push(4);
	return 0;
}
```

Compiled separately and linked together:

```
g++ -c intstack.cpp       # produces intstack.o
g++ -c main.cpp           # produces main.o
g++ intstack.o main.o -o program
```

Separate compilation is the practical payoff: change the implementation and only that one
file recompiles. Change the header and everything that includes it has to. Which tells you
where to put things.

Headers need an **include guard** so that including the same header twice does not declare the
class twice, which is a [[Compile Errors|compile error]]:

```c++
#ifndef INTSTACK_H
#define INTSTACK_H
// ...
#endif
```

This is the first module system in the degree. [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] gives
it a name and an argument ([[Coupling and Cohesion]]); [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] does the
same job with `require` and `import` in [[Node.js]], and for the same reason.
